blocks.text: Most small businesses want the same handful of AI jobs. They want to draft emails, summarize calls, read invoices, search their own documents, and make the odd image. Plenty of them can't send customer data to a cloud API to do it.

inlines.text: Most small businesses want the same handful of AI jobs. They want to draft emails, summarize calls, read invoices, search their own documents, and make the odd image. Plenty of them can't send customer data to a cloud API to do it.

blocks.text: Often the reason is data privacy and sovereignty. A clinic, a law firm, or an accountant may hold records that a contract, a regulator, or a professional duty says must stay under their control. Once that data goes to a cloud API, it sits on someone else's hardware, possibly in another jurisdiction, under terms the provider can change. Running the models on hardware you own keeps the data in your building, and lets you show an auditor exactly where it went.

blocks.text: Your n8n workflows can transcribe calls, read invoices, answer questions from your own documents, and draft replies without sending a byte to a cloud API. This post shows you how to serve every model those workflows need from one NVIDIA DGX Spark, behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint that n8n's OpenAI nodes already speak.

inlines.text: Your n8n workflows can transcribe calls, read invoices, answer questions from your own documents, and draft replies without sending a byte to a cloud API. This post shows you how to serve every model those workflows need from one NVIDIA DGX Spark, behind one OpenAI-compatible endpoint that n8n's OpenAI nodes already speak.

blocks.text: A DGX Spark has 128GB of unified memory shared by the CPU and GPU. That's enough to keep every one of those jobs loaded at once, if you pick the right models. Most of this post is about that.

inlines.text: Pick models for the bandwidth, not the parameter count

blocks.text: The DGX Spark's GB10 Grace Blackwell Superchip reads memory at 273 GB/s. When a model generates text, it reads its active weights from memory for each token, so the fewer bytes it reads, the faster it runs.

inlines.text: reads memory at 273 GB/s. When a model generates text, it reads its active weights from memory for each token, so the fewer bytes it reads, the faster it runs.

blocks.text: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model only activates a few experts per token. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B has 35B parameters in total but about 3B active. Stored in NVFP4 (NVIDIA's 4-bit floating point format), those active weights are a small fraction of a dense model's.

blocks.text: On my DGX Spark, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B generated 120 tokens per second for one user, and 359 tokens per second in total across eight users. Those numbers include the reasoning tokens the model writes before it answers.

blocks.text: Step 1: Cache everything for offline use

inlines.text: Step 1: Cache everything for offline use

blocks.text: The stack has to run with the network cable unplugged, so download every model once and record the exact commit you got. This loop caches each model and writes a lock file of repository and commit:

inlines.text: The stack has to run with the network cable unplugged, so download every model once and record the exact commit you got. This loop caches each model and writes a lock file of repository and commit:

blocks.text:
pipx install "huggingface_hub[cli]"
hf auth login

for repo in nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-4B Qwen/Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B \
            openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo zai-org/GLM-OCR Tongyi-MAI/Z-Image-Turbo; do
  hf download "$repo"
  echo "$repo $(cat ~/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--${repo//\//--}/refs/main)" >> models.lock
done

When you start a model, pass --revision with the commit from models.lock. vLLM then serves the weights you tested rather than whatever main points to today, so an upstream change can't swap the weights or the license under you.

blocks.text: This command starts the main model in vLLM:

inlines.text: This command starts the main model in vLLM:

blocks.text:
docker run -d --name qwen3.6 --gpus all --ipc=host \
  -p 172.17.0.1:8001:8000 \
  -e HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 -e VLLM_API_KEY=<your-backend-key> \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  vllm-spark:omni-0.30.0 \
  nvidia/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-NVFP4 --revision <commit-from-models.lock> \
  --served-model-name qwen3.6-35b \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.32 --max-model-len 65536 \
  --max-num-seqs 8 --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
  --trust-remote-code --kv-cache-dtype fp8 --moe-backend marlin \
  --enable-chunked-prefill --async-scheduling --enable-prefix-caching \
  --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":3,"moe_backend":"triton"}' \
  --reasoning-parser qwen3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000

blocks.text:
Using MarlinNvFp4LinearKernel for NVFP4 GEMM
Using 'MARLIN' NvFp4 MoE backend out of potential backends: ['FLASHINFER_TRTLLM', 'FLASHINFER_CUTEDSL', ...]
Your GPU does not have native support for FP4 computation but FP4 quantization is being used.

That last warning matters for how you read "NVFP4" on a DGX Spark. With this vLLM build, the weights are stored in 4 bits, but the math runs in 16 bits. You still get most of the benefit, because generating tokens is limited by reading weights from memory, and 4-bit weights are a quarter of the size. Faster FP4 kernels for GB10 may raise these numbers in later builds.

blocks.text: On a DGX Spark, the GPU and the operating system share one 128GB pool. Linux reported 121GB of it as total memory on my box. That changes two things you might take for granted on a discrete GPU.

inlines.text: On a DGX Spark, the GPU and the operating system share one 128GB pool. Linux reported 121GB of it as total memory on my box. That changes two things you might take for granted on a discrete GPU.

blocks.text: First, --gpu-memory-utilization is a fraction of the whole pool, taken at startup. It's not a fraction of what's free. An instance without a cap tries to take almost everything, and the next model fails to start.

blocks.text: LiteLLM gives every client one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Each job is a named route, so you can swap the model behind a route without touching any client. LiteLLM also handles virtual keys, teams, and budgets in its open-source version.

inlines.text: gives every client one OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Each job is a named route, so you can swap the model behind a route without touching any client. LiteLLM also handles virtual keys, teams, and budgets in its open-source version.

blocks.text: Each route in LiteLLM's config.yaml points at a backend. This excerpt shows three of them:

inlines.text: points at a backend. This excerpt shows three of them:

blocks.text:
model_list:
  - model_name: qwen3.6                 # main model: chat, coding, vision, extraction
    litellm_params:
      model: hosted_vllm/qwen3.6-35b
      api_base: http://host.docker.internal:8001/v1
      api_key: os.environ/BACKEND_API_KEY

  - model_name: whisper
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/whisper-large-v3-turbo
      api_base: http://host.docker.internal:8101/v1
      api_key: os.environ/BACKEND_API_KEY
    model_info:
      mode: audio_transcription

  - model_name: image                   # Z-Image-Turbo on vLLM-Omni
    litellm_params:
      model: openai/z-image-turbo
      api_base: http://host.docker.internal:8103/v1
      api_key: os.environ/BACKEND_API_KEY
    model_info:
      mode: image_generation

litellm_settings:
  drop_params: true                     # needed for the image route, see below

general_settings:
  master_key: os.environ/LITELLM_MASTER_KEY
  database_url: os.environ/DATABASE_URL

Keep drop_params: true. Without it, LiteLLM rejects any image request that sets response_format with a 400 error, because it doesn't map that field for a self-hosted image model. With it, LiteLLM drops the field, and vLLM-Omni returns the image as base64 anyway.

blocks.text: The backends listen only on Docker's bridge network and require a shared key, so LiteLLM is the only service on the office network. Point LiteLLM at the bridge, not at the box's LAN address. If you use the LAN address, the backends refuse the connection, because they aren't listening there.

blocks.text: Any OpenAI client now works against the DGX Spark. This Python example calls three different models through the same client:

inlines.text: Any OpenAI client now works against the DGX Spark. This Python example calls three different models through the same client:

blocks.text:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://<spark-ip>:4000/v1", api_key="<your-litellm-key>")

reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen3.6",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Draft a two-line reply confirming Tuesday's delivery."}],
)

with open("call.wav", "rb") as audio:
    transcript = client.audio.transcriptions.create(model="whisper", file=audio)

image = client.images.generate(
    model="image",
    prompt="a delivery van outside a bakery at dawn",
    size="1024x1024",
    extra_body={"num_inference_steps": 8},
)
num_inference_steps isn't an OpenAI parameter, so it goes in extra_body. LiteLLM passes it through to vLLM-Omni. The next section explains why it matters.

blocks.text: Per-user speed is the median generation speed of each request, measured after its first token. Total is all tokens generated divided by the test's elapsed time, so it also counts time to first token and any slower requests. In the single-user run, one of the five requests ran at 43 tokens per second while the other four ran at 117 to 129, which pulls the total down to 87.

blocks.text: One DGX Spark holds the whole stack, but it can't run image generation without slowing everyone's chat. For a small team, queue image jobs or run them outside working hours. Once image generation is part of the daily work, move media to a second DGX Spark and keep the first for text.

blocks.text: Model quality wasn't the hard part. Licenses were.

inlines.text: Model quality wasn't the hard part. Licenses were.

blocks.text: Several of the best open text-to-speech and image models don't allow commercial use. The FLUX models that compete with Z-Image-Turbo are non-commercial or need a separately priced license. The strongest open image model at the time of writing, Qwen-Image-2.1, ships under a research license. Some repositories even have a non-commercial twin next to a permissive original, so caching the wrong repository ID changes your license.

Pin every model to a Hugging Face commit, so a license change upstream can't land silently.
Credit CC-BY-4.0 models in your documentation.

This stack uses vLLM rather than Ollama, which ships in the starter kit. Ollama suits one person on a laptop. For a team, vLLM batches requests from many users into each pass over the weights, which is where the multi-user throughput comes from.
